title: Sangrand, the new month
hook: the first day of each month, when the Barah Maha is read and people gather

segments.voice: Yesterday, shabad, and your line: a hymn for every turn. Now the year's last stretch begins: the calendar of the banis, the days of the year that Sikhs gather around.

The first of the month comes with its own small rituals. Rent is due, the gym is suddenly full, and the calendar on the fridge flips to a new picture. It's a small fresh start that comes twelve times a year, whether you're ready or not. In many Sikh communities, the first day of the month has a name and a gathering of its own. Some who rarely make it to the gurdwara come early that morning. Today: Sangrand.
screen: `THE FIRST OF THE MONTH.` → `A SMALL FRESH START.` → `A GATHERING OF ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: Sangrand is the Punjabi form of sankranti: the day the sun moves into a new sign of the zodiac. In the traditional Punjabi calendar, that's when each solar month begins: Chet, Vaisakh, Jeth, and on through the year. You've met those months already. Earlier this year came the Barah Maha, Guru Arjan's song of the twelve months in Raag Majh, where each month becomes a stage in the soul's longing for the Beloved. On Sangrand, many gurdwaras read that month's stanza aloud, so the sangat begins the month with its verse: in Chet, the Chet stanza; in Vaisakh, the Vaisakh stanza. Families come for kirtan, Ardas and langar. A fair question: does the Granth say some days are holier than others? Guru Arjan answers inside the Barah Maha itself. Near the end, on Ang one thirty-six, he says, in paraphrase: the months, the days, the moments are blessed for those on whom the Lord casts His glance of grace. So the date isn't magic. What makes a day good is remembering God in it. Sikhs hold that in different ways. Many love Sangrand as a chance to begin the month in sangat. Others, including some Sikh scholars and reformers, prefer not to make the date itself special, and say every day is the same before God. Both look to the same line, and both agree on what it asks: whatever the date, begin it remembering.
screen: `SANKRANTI: THE SUN'S NEW SIGN.` · `THE MONTH'S STANZA, READ ALOUD.` · `GRACE MAKES THE DAY BLESSED.` · `BEGIN THE MONTH REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `THE MONTH BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Find out, or guess, which Punjabi month you're in, and look back over the past month: one thing to leave behind, one to carry forward. Then picture the first morning of next month, begun with remembering: a line read, a visit, a quiet minute. If you pray, you can say Waheguru to open the new month.
Sangrand. The first day of a Punjabi solar month, when the sun enters a new sign, and many gurdwaras read that month's stanza of the Barah Maha.
Your line: the month begins. Twelve small fresh starts a year. That's day six hundred eighty-one.
